questions.cardText:
[Mathematics] In statistics, what is the “mode”?
A. The middle value in a list of numbers
B. The average of a list of numbers
C. The most frequent number in a list
Answer: C.
questions.de: Wie heißt in der Statistik der Wert, der in einem Datensatz am häufigsten vorkommt?
questions.en: In statistics, what is the value that appears most often in a set of data called?

timeline.labelEn: Karl Pearson introduces the statistical term 'mode'
timeline.labelDe: Karl Pearson führt den statistischen Begriff „Modus“ (mode) ein

questions.notes: Card asks for the definition; reworked so the definition is the clue and the term the answer. Confirmed; the term dates from Karl Pearson (1895). German also 'Modalwert'.

questions.cardText:
[Musicology] Which of the following best describes a piece with “sonata” in its title?
A. A traditional folk ballad
B. An ensemble piece for a chamber orchestra
C. A classical composition for an instrumental soloist, often with piano accompaniment
Answer: C. Paradoxically, a piece with “sonata” in its title is not always a sonata, and sonatas do not always include “sonata” in the title.
questions.de: Wie heißt die klassische Instrumentalkomposition, meist in drei oder vier Sätzen, für ein Soloinstrument (oft ein Tasteninstrument) oder für einen Solisten mit Klavierbegleitung?
questions.en: What is the name of the classical instrumental composition, usually in three or four movements, written for a solo instrument (often a keyboard) or for a soloist accompanied by piano?

timeline.labelEn: The Classical era, when the sonata became the basic form for large-scale instrumental works
timeline.labelDe: Die Wiener Klassik, in der die Sonate zur Grundform großer Instrumentalwerke wurde

questions.notes: Card's 'which best describes' reworked to ask the term from the description. Confirmed: after the Baroque, most works called sonatas are for a solo instrument (most often keyboard) or a solo instrument accompanied by keyboard; Baroque sonatas could be for one or more instruments with continuo. Timeline: Classical period, conventional dates c. 1750–1820.
